utterances.text: Thank you. That's why I'm asking you. Such individuals, if they are suspects, they would be then escorted and handed over to the Prizren SUP for further processing, for the crime report to be submitted and so on?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are fixed procedures what needs to be done. There are dead-lines that have to be met. So first of all, a policeman who would bring in someone would have to explain why the person was brought in, then the person would have to be searched and so on. Then interviewed and then there would be a decision on their detention issued, written decision, and then that person, following such a decision, would be detained. Now, whether these people actually complied with the procedure and acted on it, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Being in the administration, did you have anything to do with this type of procedure?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And who was in charge of processing the papers for such a suspect who was brought in to Suva Reka OUP?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would be a paper that would have to be issued when a person is brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All I would like to know is the paperwork. Who would do the paperwork, fill out the forms, the necessary forms, the log-book where the name would be entered, and so on? Who would be in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the log-book for persons who are detained can be -- actually, the decision to detain a person who is brought into the station would be something that could be issued by the commander, the deputy commander, or the assistant. And then they would further process and issue the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So this was not done by the duty service; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Now, I'm not sure whether this would be written down in the log-book that a person was brought in as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, who would be in charge of a suspect, of a person who was brought in as a suspect and kept in this room for detention? Who is responsible for this person?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the authorised person, once a decision, a written decision was issued, would be the shift leader at the duty service. And he was duty-bound to inform the following shift leader, the shift leader coming after him, to inform him of a person being detained and what type of detention it is and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us, please, you were in the office of the duty service, what happened next? What can you recall?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly which one of my colleagues picked up the key that hung above the desk of the shift leader, and I can't recall who it was exactly who picked up this key which was hanging there. The key to the room for detention. But I remember clearly that they took this key, they unlocked the room, they took this man out, and he was taken out into the hallway from this room marked with number 4, brought to the spot where it says number 1. And then they did not enter the duty service office, rather he turned right and then went toward the place marked with number 6 and then around the corner to the place marked with number 5 where an APC was parked some 10 metres from the corner of the building where number 134/98 is written down. And from this office of the duty service, I heard, because it was not too far away, I heard a shot. I can't remember if it was a pistol or a rifle shot, whether there was one or several shots. And when I went out, I mean, it immediately occurred to me that I was suspicious. I had suspicions that they wanted to shoot this man. And when I reached the corner of the building, the building of the Suva Reka police station, I saw this man dead and next to him was Radovan Tanovic, Sladjan Cukaric and Miroslav Petkovic, they were standing there next to him. I don't know who it was of the three who shot him. They would know that better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you heard this shot but you didn't see it actually happening. What happened from the moment when you heard the shot to the time when you got out of the office?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was just a few seconds, let's say 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did the three of them do when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing, they were just standing by this man and they were not doing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, now, what happened next.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I went back to the duty service office and then some five to ten minutes later, as I've already told you, I heard a burst of gun-fire coming from the direction of Restanski Put or thereabouts, and then I went out. I was on the sidewalk as I described this yesterday, of Cara Dusana Street, and then I saw the things that I described yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you didn't know nor did you see when you went back to the duty service office, where they went?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you just reacted because you heard the sound of gun-shots or shots; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this do you know who Milica Djordjevic is?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that the person who was detained was taken to the house that you earlier marked with number 2 and shot there, shot dead there?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what he claimed in Belgrade, and I think you were one of the Defence team of one of the accused there, so he claimed that this man was taken to that house and that from the bell tower he saw that Sladjan Cukaric had shot the man. On the other hand, he also claimed that I was not in Suva Reka on that particular day at all. So that his entire statement to me is simply suspicious, or it lacks credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you this: If you were at the spot marked with number 2 and he was at the spot where the bell tower was, this distance would have been approximately the same as the distance -- so the distance from the bell tower to house number 2 and from where you were to number 2 was approximately the same, and the line of vision was approximately the same?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I saw some people standing there and that -- you could also see on the sketch that I made, and also it could be seen from the bell tower because there were some windows there and anyone who had good vision could see it. Although, I stand by what I said. And I said that this man, who had been detained, was shot next to the building of the Suva Reka OUP. And I stand by that. Whether they said something else, I don't know, but I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us this: When you heard the shots, you went to the spot outside the bus terminal. Tell us this: Was someone --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction: In front of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, was anyone with you while you were there outside the police station when you heard the shots and you went out onto the street outside the police station, was there anyone there with you?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, but I think there wasn't anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was there anything on the street as you got out of the building?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was only a vehicle parked by a lamp post, that was the vehicle containing the bodies of the dead members of the Berisha family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was the vehicle there when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got out to see which family they were killing, the vehicle was already there. Now, when it had been brought there, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me, please, other than the parked truck, was there anything else on the road?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, and I can't say with any certainty whether there was or wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude then that you don't know where this truck had come from, the parked truck that you saw there when you left the building?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can. I can't say exactly from which direction it had come, but for reasons of security, I concluded that it could only have come from the direction of Prizren because the Pristina direction was quite dangerous already.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, could they have come from the part where the municipal building was or the Balkan building was?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's all from the direction of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they could have come from some spot in Suva Reka; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This was all in Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, how long did you stay there outside the police station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, but I think it wasn't very long. Maybe a minute or so that I lingered there at the spot where the sidewalk was and where this parked truck was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. So what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next I went back to the station -- into the station, and then, I can't remember who it was who told me to go and load the bodies because the bodies had to be buried, so then I went to the administration office to take my rifle. I'm not sure if I had my pistol on me already. Then I got ready. I locked up the administration room and went behind this truck to load the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't remember exactly where it was that you set off from but you remember you took the rifle, and then again, you had to walk out through the station courtyard, so what happened next?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I'm saying is that this detained person was lying there dead. His body was lying there. And then I loaded this body together with a colleague who was a protected witness here, we loaded him onto the truck and then the truck went in the direction of Restane.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you next turn to page K04085.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The sketch of the police station that has been marked, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I asked for that to be copied and translated. I don't know whether we can mark it as such for identification. There's very little to translate, and we had the witness explain everything. Therefore, I seek to tender it. If that cannot be met, then perhaps we could have it MFI'd pending translation. Of course, the marked numbers will be missing, but then they can be copied as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the marked page as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00310.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, please go to page 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the bottom, the fourth and third lines, can you read out the question and the answer?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which sentence exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The investigative judge and what happened and then what follows.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigative judge: "What happened with the corpse of the detainee?" Witness: "He was taken away on a truck. I don't know where to."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Veljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 11 of the English, I apologise for having omitted to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it you are referring to the transcript of the questioning by Judge Dilparic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the same statement. I have a translation for the other one, that was provided to the Prosecution. So we have a number for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, in 2004 you said that the body was taken away on a truck and that you didn't know where to. This is a transcript.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects what I said. I put it that way at that time. I forgot some things and now I put it differently, so that's a problem then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, is your recollection better now or was it better back then since that was closer to the events?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be illogical for me to say that my recollection is better now since more time has elapsed, but I would like to stand by what I just said and that is that we put the body on the truck and that together with the Berisha family, that body was buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this is the type of event that is difficult to forget, it is in the your run-of-the-mill day? You see a corpse like that and it remains etched in your memory?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but the situation in which I was there doing it with my work-mates was such that some things remain etched in my memory whereas others I seem to have easily forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that response.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please provide the witness with his statement given to the Prosecution on the 18th of January, 2006. I have it in B/C/S. Your Honours, and Mr. Stamp, this is 65 ter 05337.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, look at the end of paragraph 18, it is page 5 in the English. Here you say in the sentence mentioning the pizzeria, I quote: "There was a crime technician officer present at the pizzeria named Todor Jovanovic though I did not see him conducting any sort of investigation." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, the problem we have is that my statements, well, I shouldn't overstate it, but let's say half of it does not tally. I included some things that others had said. Those who questioned me were far more versed in the very core of the problem in the case itself, and they prompted me, and I then consented that certain things be introduced into my statement. I cannot say with any certainty whether there was a scene-of-crime officer there by the name of Todor Jovanovic or not. If several people said so. In my view, he wasn't there. As for any others, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, I want to only hear from you about the things you know and saw. When you were referring to someone else, then, of course, you can warn us about that. Let's clear one thing up: This statement you signed in English, was it read back to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Serbian. I signed every page of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But you signed the English pages, correct, not the Serbian ones?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I do think that I only signed the English copy, not the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't think that is in dispute. We have it here. And you had no objections when it was being read back to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I signed without any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Given the time that has passed, there may have been more ideas and combinations that came to your mind since then, this is the third statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the fourth at Jevrem Grujica, number 11. If we do not count the Leskovac statement, then it is the third. If we do, then this is the fourth statement. I gave a statement in Leskovac in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you gave the first statement to the police, they also shared information with you to the effect that they knew certain things?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they put question, I provided answers, but they also added things, and I simply believed them. I should believe the person interviewing me. If I don't trust you, who should I trust?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You should trust the court alone.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So next we have another statement before an investigative judge, and he referred to what you had said to the police?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Judge Dilparic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that they showed me any statements by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean statements of others. He referred to your first statement given to the police and that you based your evidence on that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. He may have shown me that statement, but I can't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you go to page 68. Have a look at the beginning of this statement.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The fourth paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigative judge: "In the statement to the police you said you had seen him at the time as you were loading the bodies before the business centre, Commander Repanovic and Milojko [phoen] came." Witness's answer: "So he was there as well?" Investigative judge: "I don't know. This is what you said to the police." Witness: "He was probably there if I said so. I signed several pages, so he must have been there, it must have been like that."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you were shown your statement to the police on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. This is what I conclude based on my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This brings us to your third statement given in September.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you provided that statement because you were called to do that by the war crimes investigator in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was summoned by the deputy state attorney in Leskovac and he did say that that was for the purposes of the war crimes bench. He told me that I was supposed to give a new statement. Since I resided closer to Leskovac than Belgrade, he said that I should give that statement in Leskovac, you will sign it and I will take a copy to Belgrade. Before I started giving that statement, I saw a list of people who were supposed to be apprehended. As for the other two statements, there was no plan to apprehend any persons, but just prior to giving this third statement, I saw on the Judge's desk that there was a list of those who were supposed to be detained. I conclude from that that he was filling in the gaps because he was much more acquainted with the whole case. That was his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you went to Jevrem Grujica Street?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I gave the statement in Leskovac, in addition to having read the list of people who were supposed to be detained, after signing the statement, the deputy district attorney in Leskovac, Mr. Stankovic, officially told me that people were going to detained. And I can even quote him. He said, Your statement tallies completely in the most important aspects with those of other witnesses. It only deviates in some small detail which are -- is not that relevant. He put to me then that a woman from that family survived. That she jumped off the truck in Prizren. She went to a Serbian who promised to appear here as a witness. He also said that the corpses were taken to the Prizren barracks where they were buried for two weeks. Two weeks later, they were reburied at Batajnica. He concluded by saying, Go home; you will be called to appear during the main hearing which will be recorded. He simply let me know that the people on the list will apprehended. You know, from your colleague in Belgrade I was criticized by the media because I referred to certain media articles, et cetera. The colleagues in Medvedje knew where I worked and were familiar with my statements, and three weeks later, they told me, Some of your people are detained. People usually say that journalists lie, but they didn't lie a thing about this case. I did read that they were detained and charged with the murders of the Berisha family, and the papers only carried initials those -- of those detained. I was familiar with the initials, and when I was told this I was quite shocked in the courtroom. And then I said openly, These people are counting their last days of freedom. And that was correct. Three weeks after my Leskovac statement, nine people ended up in the investigative prison in Belgrade that was on the 17th of October, 2005. I gave my statement on the 23rd of September, 2005. On the 17th of October - says the witness - maybe before that, maybe after that, they were already in jail in Belgrade. Later on in January, I received a summons via my superior in Medvedje to appear in Jevrem Grujica Street on number 11 to have -- to attend a new hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Mr. Veljkovic, let us go back to several things. When you were in Leskovac with Mr. Dragoljub Stankovic, there you said your famous statement which goes something like: If others say he was there, then he must have been.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If that was in 2005 as you say, in September, then in January 2006 you went to Jevrem Grujica Street?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And those people you referred to were put in jail in October 2006?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people were detained in 2005, not 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: 2005, you're right. In January you gave a statement to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It was translated and you signed it. You say that they showed you certain statements, et cetera. Is it correct that you never attended any meetings of those in charge of the OUP in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you never attended the meetings of those in charge of the police station in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you never attended any meetings of those in charge of the OUP in the territory of Prizren as well as the chief of police in the Prizren SUP?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you were issued tasks and that you reported to the Prizren SUP?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of each month, I submitted reports on those brought in, on those whose IDs were checked, as well as on the reports and Official Notes recorded. I took that to Nenad Jovanovic who was the assistant commander. It would be sent by mail on a monthly basis to Prizren. They kept all the records about the work of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the head of the police station, Mr. Repanovic, was in direct communication only with Prizren?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a head, he was the station commander. And yes, he did. When he was absent, there was his deputy and his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have document D004-2264.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, what will be presented to you is an extract from the daily event or incidents log of the Suva Reka police station for 1999. The period concerned is the 13th of March to -- sorry, the 26th of February, 1999, to, let me see, to the 27th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 36. I think it is page 3. Yes. Can we please go down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see the entry numbers 36?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What is registered there? Just describe it for us, it will be translated.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll read it out, although it is a bit unclear. It is reported -- no, first of all: "Terrorism Article 125 of the Penal Code of Serbia. This was done by Nebojsa Gogic, traffic policeman, who was an employee in the Suva Reka station. He reports that in Cara Dusana Street in Suva Reka in the auto spare parts shop in Retimlje," if I'm reading that correctly, "Balkom Belt [phoen] was killed by terrorists as well as Nenad Lazic from the village of Sopina. Shots were fired from a handgun and then" - what does it say here? - "from close proximity." An on-site investigation was done by the investigative judge, a dispatch was sent to Prizren, a criminal report was submitted and there's no number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page. Entry number 37. What is the date?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th of April at 2100 hours. Sorry, 2110. Nenad Jovanovic, assistant commander of the Suva Reka police station. Terrorist attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a translation of it. Am I right in saying that as of the 22nd of March under item 36 and up to the 5th of April, 1999, item 37, there was not a single incident that was reported in the daily incidents book?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that everything entered into the daily incidents log was something that the SUP in Prizren was notified about?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that a dispatch was sent. However, I do think that they first reported that by phone and then would send dispatches. I am familiar with this event concerning Nenad Jovanovic. I went to the scene. A terrorist used a hand-held launcher. It hit their vehicle, but fortunately none of the colleagues were hurt. Even Nenad Jovanovic was there himself. It was in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You were there. Who was in the vehicle with Nenad Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramiz Papic and someone else. Certainly there wasn't only one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree with me that based on this daily incidents log-book, the police station did not inform the Prizren SUP of the murder of the Berisha family?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- you mean when the Berisha family were killed? No, I can't really say for certain whether they informed Prizren or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Should such an incident be logged in the daily incidents log-book?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question because, simply put, it is exceeding one's -- well, it's an instance of exceeding of authority without any prior intention, and I wouldn't really know what that description of the incident would actually look like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did the Suva Reka police station actually conceal this event, the events of the 26th of March in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really say that either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, please tell us, when you returned to the station, did you receive an order, did anyone issue an order to you that you should go and send or expel Albanians from their homes?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there, I heard that it was said that people should not be killed, that we should go from door to door and order the people of ethnic Albanian origin to leave their homes, to leave Suva Reka, and to go to Albania freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this, who could you have heard this from when you were at the police station all by yourself?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall which colleague it was who told me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that this was something that you were just discussing amongst yourselves?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And am I correct in saying that you did not leave the station in order to go and inform the Albanians of that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I did not go to tell Albanians to leave their homes, but I told you yesterday, and I stand by it, that I was at the police station when there was this phone call where the woman asked me about this order to move out; and when she asked me, Where should we go, and I said, Go abroad, and when she said, Well whom do we have in Albania, to which I said, Well, in that case the same fate will meet you that met the Berisha family. And then I hung up. Then about half an hour later, I don't know if even that much time passed, people just started packing and leaving for Albania en masse in their cars and so on. So this would have been -- this would have taken place for about an hour or so. It couldn't have been more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Veljkovic, did you tell the ICTY investigator about this when you provided your statement in 2006?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. I don't even know if the gentleman asked me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you read, please -- would you please read paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When we returned to the police station I heard from other colleagues that another order had been given that we were to go from house to house and tell any remaining Albanians that they have half an hour to pack their things and leave. I assumed that this order also had come from Repanovic. I just stayed in the police station. Half an hour later, the Albanians began to leave in their vehicles towards Prizren or the border with Albania."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it -- would it be possible for an ICTY investigator to not note down something that you may have said about this in January 2006?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean whether he would have written it down, I can't really know, but I don't even remember whether he put that question or not. But I know that I was asked about it by the gentleman who interviewed me the first time, the 26 or 27th February, 2003, when toward the end of the interview he asked me, and I recall the question: "What did you say to the woman who called the duty service of the Suva Reka police station?" He put that question directly to me, and then I said that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: What language did you speak when you spoke to this woman?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbian because I can't speak Albanian. And when she called, she asked me in Serbian. I didn't know, of course, who was tall calling; she just asked that, and I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you do not have any knowledge, direct knowledge, about -- that you were never told that Albanian nationals should move out?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct when I say that you did not receive an order to go and tell the people of Albanian ethnicity that they should move out?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the statement 65 ter 337, I seek that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the date of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the statement of 18th January, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00311.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, do you remember that during the war an investigating team would go in the field to investigate -- to conduct an on-site investigation if a criminal report was submitted?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember only one incident when an on-site investigation was conducted by an investigating judge and with the assistance of the police. And the outcome of this investigation was very tragic. This was at the end of the air-strike campaign. I think this was in late May, in the second half of May, and I know well that I was on duty at the time. And at about 2.00 or 3.00, I was told by our patrols via our communication line that there was a murder in Pecane or somewhere like that, I can't exactly recall where. And so our men decided that on the next day they would go there and conduct an on-site investigation. When they were leaving, the commander -- the deputy commander of Prokuplje was there, I think his driver was there too, and the Prizren investigating Judge Cane Janicijevic; and on their way out, they ran into a land-mine and all three were killed. Whether there were any other on-site investigations before that, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't asking you only about the deaths of non-Albanians, but also Albanians. When there were Albanians found dead in Suva Reka, there would be a team to investigate the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have document D004-2246, please, on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, this is a report from April 1st on the finding of a body in Prizrenska Street in Suva Reka. Do you recall the incident?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall it. I did not keep records of crime reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But do you recall that there was an investigating team toward the end of March that was conducting an investigation on Restanski Road?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 30th of March, and they were conducting an investigation between the houses of the Berisha family?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know of Dr. Boban Sanovic [as interpreted] and how he got killed?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was in the first half of April, 1999. He was with four of his colleagues, people from the Territorial Defence, and they were on their way to -- between Stopina-Musotiste [phoen] on the main road, Albanian terrorists carried out an armed attack on them. I think there were five men in this vehicle including Dr. Boban, and they were killed. I don't know if they conducted an on-site investigation or not. They were brought to the medical centre first, and then I can't say with certainty what happened afterwards, whether their bodies were taken to Prizren or not to the forensic institute to be examined. And I think on the very next day they were buried. So I recall this incident vividly. I think this would have been around 1.00 p.m., but I'm not sure of the date, but I know it was in the first half of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Veljkovic, thank you for answering my questions. Your Honours, I thank you and this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see, Mr. Djurdjic has had another thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I forgot to seek to tender the daily incidents log, to have it MFI'd pending translation. This was document -- it was a Defence document. We saw it. If you bear with me, and I apologise to my learned friend Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is D004-2264.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00312 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we are at it, the untranslated documents marked for translation, we had taken a position when this procedure started that we would not object because we wanted to the procedures to move quickly, but over the last two weeks the majority of the documents the Defence has used are not in the language of the Tribunal and it is becoming -- or any of the official languages, and it is becoming very difficult to follow the evidence of the witness with these untranslated documents. Now, I know that there are difficulties in getting documents translated, but it seems to me that if the Defence made proper representations to the CLSS, or whoever does the translations, and prior to that prioritised documents in the order that we were going to use them, we could have translated documents used with the witnesses while they are here. I discovered in respect to one document when I had a spot translation after the witness left that if there was a translation there would be meaningful information that we could have brought before the Court. So I would ask the Court if -- and this is just a request made to the Defence through the Court, if proper efforts could be made to have documents in the language of the Tribunal used in cross-examination. I know it can be done because these are not many documents, and I've seen situations in the past where five times as many documents have been translated by counsel, and that is just a matter not of sending simply a batch of documents for translation, but of prioritizing them. It can be done. And if the Defence do what is necessary, we will have documents that we can read. That's all I wish to say about it now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, and Mr. Djurdjic, the Chamber would ask you to liaise on this matter and to do it with the CLSS in an effort to ensure that the occasions when an untranslated document is used are kept to a minimum. It has become apparent that not merely an isolated document, but quite consistently, most documents put by the Defence to witnesses in cross-examination have not been translated. The Chamber has, of course, left it open to the Prosecution in such a case to seek to recall the witness at a later time when a translation is made, but we all realise that the cost and delay involved in such a process is considerable and that it would only be a really grave matter that would warrant that occurring. Therefore, we would ask that the present position be improved dramatically by whatever means can be arranged in cooperation with the CLSS. Obviously if this is not done, the Chamber's recourse will have to be to refuse to allow the use of untranslated documents which will be much to the disadvantage, I would expect, of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, briefly, I think Mr. Stamp is right, although, I believe that the translation service is doing utmost. I forward them a voluminous bulk of documents, but the problem may have been that we did not prioritize adequately. We will do so in the future. However, the documents we showed to the witnesses were more of an illustrative nature than material to the issues at hand. In any case, we will try to meet the request put to us. As regards the translation service, we certainly have no objections as to their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Veljkovic, that there was an armoured personnel carrier outside the police station on the 26th. To which unit did it belong?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The APC belonged to the OUP in Suva Reka. But I can't say with any certainty that that vehicle was there solely for the purposes of the special unit of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take it from your answer that it was sometimes used for the purposes of the special unit of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense? Special units are one thing and PJPs are another.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Line 22 should read special unit, of the PJP. Basically meaning the same thing. The special unit, the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So it was sometimes used by the PJP?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty whether it was or was not used by the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move on to something else, and I'm referring to page 33 of today's record. You were asked by counsel about the persons who were present with you when you went with the truck to load bodies. And you read from what you had said to the investigating judge. And while you were being questioned about it, you think -- I think you said you might have been confused then about the persons who travelled with you, and you referred to your first statement. I would, with the leave of the Court, like to give you a copy of your first statement and just ask if this assists you to remember who went with you and who you saw at the cafe when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I could briefly show him this first statement, this statement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And copy for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please switch off his microphone when not using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The date of this statement, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a statement of the 27th of February, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Made to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To the MUP, the MUP officials at the MUP office in Belgrade, Kneza Milosa Street, number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall giving that statement, Mr. Veljkovic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. That was my first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think you signed all the pages of that statement as well?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you look at the last page and the last two sentences, you attested that: "This statement has been read out to me, I hereby verify its accuracy and accept it as mine and I am therefore signing it as such. I also state that during the interview conducted by the MUP officials of the Republic of Serbia I was not subjected to any form of violence or pressure." That is what you attested to?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just want to remind you of what is at -- is on the statement. If you could look at the last sentence of page 2. And my question will be: Does this remind you of who was it who accompanied you when you went with the truck to pick up bodies? But I want you to just go through it first before answering that question and try to remember. The last sentence of page 2, can you read that sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "After that, the aforementioned policemen were in pursuit, still shooting at the people fleeing. Commander Repanovic ordered me and Ivica Novkovic who was a reservist who hailed from Dubovo, from Prokuplje, to collect the bodies, he also said that a truck was to come to load the bodies onto it." Is that the sentence you had in mind on page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you move to page 3. And just read the first sentence but a little bit more slowly now, a little bit more slowly because it has to be translated. The first sentence of page 3.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When Ivica Novkovic and I arrived close to the house which used to house the OSCE, a truck came from the direction of Restane with two uniformed people inside. I think they were reservists from Suva Reka. The names of those persons in the truck is something I do not know. I do think I could recognise them if shown their photographs."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, if you move on to the first -- to the second paragraph of page 3 and read the first two sentences. Or could you just read slowly the second paragraph of page 3.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We boarded the truck and set out for Lestane [as interpreted]. We arrived at the first intersection when the truck made a U-turn. Ivica Novkovic and I were following the truck on foot, loading the bodies close to the intersection. There were five or six of them. I remember there were some corpses that we could not load onto the truck because they were too heavy. We left those behind. There was a carpenter's shop on Miladina Popovica Street close to the crossroads. We didn't take all of the corpses from the shop. There was another charred body at the entrance of the shop. After that, the truck went back to the OUP building. Ivica Novkovic and I followed. I think when passed by the former OSCE house where we loaded some ten bodies, we left some of them behind as well. Then the truck turned towards the small businesses centre along the main road between Prizren and Pristina, whereas Ivica Novkovic and I went on foot towards the direction from which we could hear shots and hand-grenade explosions."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you also read the next paragraph slowly. It's a short paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When we arrived before a pizzeria at the small businesses centre, the name of which I no longer remember, but I do know that it was across the street from the Metohija Vino company, we came across a parked truck, the trailer of which was turned toward the pizzeria entrance. I saw the policeman Miroslav Tanovic and Petkovic as well as a policeman by the nickname of Tzece [phoen] he stood next to a kiosk vis-a-vis the municipal building at the small businesses centre. We also found Dr. Boban Vuksanovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having read what you said in your first statement, do you now recall who it was who travelled with you when you went with the truck on the road to pick up the bodies?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was such a long time ago. I cannot say with a hundred per cent certainty that Ivica Novkovic and another colleague were with me as of the moment when we started loading the body that was in the courtyard of the OUP in Suva Reka and until we finished. Still, I stand by what I said and that is that I began forgetting things, and that the statement is as I had it originally, that is to say that myself and the two reservists went towards Restanski Put to load the bodies. Whether there were some other corpses that belonged to the Berisha family and whether these Albanians may have been attacking the police and killed in response, that is something I cannot say any longer. But I would still like to be stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not talking or asking you to focus on the bodies now. Just the police accompanying you. You note in this statement that you -- on many occasions, you only refer to Ivica Novkovic as the one person who accompanied you. Does that not assist you to remember?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does assist me to remember, but - because I remember that he refused to load any bodies - but I stand by what I said about the other reserve policemen, that he was there with me loading the bodies because I could not have possibly done it on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we move into private session, Your Honour. I just have one question I'd like to ask in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Stamp was critical of my conduct and yet here we see for the second time he is using a document for which there is no translation, and secondly, he used a document that was not used earlier during the examination-in-chief, so I would like to be given the opportunity to put to the witness some issues that are in this new document after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, do you suggest this document was used during cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not suggest that it was used during cross-examination. The witness just referred to his first statement in a context as if to suggest it might well be said that that would explain what he was saying. This is a statement that had been disclosed to Defence some time ago. I just brought a courtesy copy for them. And there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your submission is that you merely referred to a statement to see if it assisted the witness's recollection?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there a reason you didn't do that in your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It did not arise then. What I did arose from what the witness said in cross-examination in response to a question from a friends about the order of the statements and the statements that were given. This is something that arose entirely in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have run out of time on the tape. So we must adjourn now, and we will continue at 10 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber, strictly the reference made to the statement was not to the contents of the statement by Mr. Djurdjic. The extent to which reference was made by Mr. Stamp in having the witness refresh his memory was such that in the view of the Chamber, it would be appropriate to allow Mr. Djurdjic, given his limited use of the -- or reference to the statement, to be able now to renew his cross-examination to deal with any aspect of the statement. That, in turn, may enliven a further opportunity to re-exam, Mr. Stamp. We will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I have been given another opportunity thanks to Mr. Stamp to discuss with you your statement provided to the administration for fighting organised crime on the 27th of February, 2003. Would you please take a look at the last page of this statement because you have gone through the whole statement with Mr. Stamp, and tell me whether you see at the end of this statement that any mention is made of this woman that you told me about beforehand?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whom who survived the shooting?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, the woman who made the phone call to the station. I believe it should be on page 23 or so, so would you take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me explain it to you. They put questions to me and then they wrote down my answers in a notebook. And when I completed my statement, they said that I had to wait there for them to type the statement over and enter it in the computer, and then I would have to sign the statement. So then I waited for about an hour or so while they wrote down the statement, and then they printed it out and gave it to me to sign. I did not read it at the time, I admit that. I just signed it. And if they chose to omit any mention of this woman who called the station, well, they would know why that is so. I wouldn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not dwell too much on this. Here it says: "This statement has been read over to me and it is true and it reflects my words, and as such I sign it." So in other words, it was read out it to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I signed the statement and it says there that it was read back to me, then it's probably my error. I probably, in that case, did not want to insist on it and ask them why they didn't enter the portion about the woman who called on the phone. But you see, they also asked me about the murder of a man at the gas station, and I told them that I didn't know of that and it was the first time that I heard of that from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, I've already asked you about it, you forgot, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this statement into evidence rather than go over it paragraph by paragraph because I think that it's been read almost in its entirety, and if not, perhaps Mr. Veljkovic could read the third paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean the paragraph beginning with once we completed -- "Once we completed loading the bodies we returned to the Suva Reka OUP." All right, I'd start over. "When we finished loading the bodies around 3.00" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Hold it there for a moment, please. You propose to put a question to the witness about this paragraph? You do, very well, read it if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "When we finished loading the bodies, around 3.00 p.m. I returned to the OUP building in Suva Reka. A little later, I heard that an order had been issued to the effect that Albanians should not be killed any more, and that it was ordered that we should go from house to house and tell them that they should leave their houses within 30 minutes for Albania, and if not, that they would be killed. I don't know who issued this order."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Veljkovic. Was this part of your statement? Does it reflect correctly the words that you used?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So I seek again to admit this into evidence, although I'm not quite sure whether it has been translated yet, Your Honours, because I haven't seen it. I didn't see it on the screen either now or when Mr. Stamp was questioning the witness, and if it does not exist, then I suggest that it be marked for identification. Or in the alternative, if we have the translation then -- well, I've just been told by Ms. O'Leary that we do have a translation but apparently it's not been entered into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statement we are told has been translated. It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, any further re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No re-examination further to those questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, I have a short question for you. This morning you told us about the bodies in the pizzeria, this is page 22, line 13, and the following. You said: "This was a great deal of bodies and there would have been an outbreak if we had left them. If we had left them, there would be many more accused and people prosecuted than there already were." I didn't understand this answer. Perhaps you can explain it a little bit more. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant is that the bodies that were in the pizzeria could not be left there. They had to be buried somewhere to prevent -- to prevent an outbreak of disease. Now, when we left Suva Reka later on, which we did, if it was -- if it was discovered then that people had been killed and had been left behind, there was the possibility that an even greater number of people would be indicted, not only for the killing of these people, but also for not burying their bodies but just leaving them behind. That is what I meant and that is my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked about the interview by the investigative judge in Belgrade, Mr. Dilparic, and twice you told the Chamber that you were frightened or scared in that situation, during your examination there. Can you tell us in which way you have been frightened and what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was anxious and afraid simply because I was fearing for my freedom. When you are called for questioning, you receive a summons as a regular citizens and it is very easy or it might very easily turn into you becoming a suspect. That was the first thing. The second thing is I was afraid also because I felt very uncomfortable testifying against the people who were my co-workers, although, what they did, they did deliberately and with premeditation. But I saw that in this case, many witnesses have been questioned, and I realised that there was nothing that I could conceal. That there was simply, in addition to active policemen, there were also reservists who were called to testify, and of course they would not allow it. They wouldn't let it happen that my testimony jeopardized their freedom. So that was part of the reason why I was afraid and not because your colleague Dilparic was in any way unkind to me or anything to that effect. So that was the sole reason for my feeling of anxiety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: When you were following the truck going along the Restanski Put Road --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Whose decision was it to make the U-turn when you were following the truck?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only person there was the driver of the truck. He was the one who made that decision. No one else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Did you ask him why he made that decision?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Did you want to know?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That concludes the questioning for you. You are now free to return to your normal activities, and the Court Officer will show you out. We would thank you for your attendance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, Mr. Coo, as I understand it, is the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: His evidence is unlikely to be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it's unlikely to be this brief. And I did want to raise a matter of scheduling with you in light of the point we are at this time. I would prefer if we could do him in one go as it were. Because of the nature of his evidence, I think it would be more efficient if we can do him in the same day. If we start now, I understand you have a witness tomorrow who needs to be on and done and I think then we would have to put Mr. Coo off to maybe follow late tomorrow afternoon or some other day. I would prefer if we could just recess today and reschedule Mr. Coo for another time when it's mutually convenient to everyone. I had some conversation with my learned friend Mr. Djordjevic during the most recent break about that. I think the later he is scheduled, actually the shorter his evidence may be because some exhibits that are on the list I have for him may come in through other witnesses before we get there. So, in essence, that's my request at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we certainly see that to commence him now for just over 15 minutes is not going to be very practical, and the witness scheduled for tomorrow is a witness of some substance. We certainly anticipate he will finish within the day, but again, it might be a situation somewhat similar to today. So to complicate matters, the Prosecution planning is for a series of witnesses, three, to give evidence by videolink Monday and Tuesday, even it was thought perhaps Wednesday, but we would think it ought to be possible in two days to finish those three witnesses. So the earliest opportunity would be the last days of next week or even at some later time if other witnesses are available that would fill out the time profitably next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a personal interest, I would like to appear before you all again and I'm actually leaving tomorrow and won't be in town and then I'm out Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday the following week. And I understand that the week of July 20th you are only sitting Monday, Tuesday, and part of Wednesday. So it may be that I'll see if Mr. Coo can be available August 17th or some date shortly thereafter. And try to schedule him then if that's convenient to him and to you and Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, Mr. Hannis. We look forward to hearing you again at some time. We will have to content ourselves in patience waiting for that event. Mr. Djurdjic, I'm sure, will learn from Ms. O'Leary of our deliberations and reasons. We certainly indicate to counsel that the witness tomorrow, we would expect to be finished in the course of tomorrow and all counsel should keep that in their time planning and that we would anticipate on Wednesday of next week to reach the next non-videolink witness. That being so, we therefore adjourn for the day to resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 10th day of July, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.31 p.m.
